introduction-the-invisible-price-tag.core: In the cloud, any engineer can create expensive infrastructure with a few lines of code, and nobody sees the cost until the bill arrives weeks later. That delay breaks the feedback loop: whoever made the change has moved on. Shifting cost left means showing the price of a change at review time, when it is cheapest to adjust.

first_principles.problem: A PR changing instance_type from m5.large to m5.8xlarge across 20 nodes is approved without anyone noticing a $20k/month increase.

analogy.title: A shopping cart that shows the total before checkout
analogy.story: Imagine shopping with no prices until the credit-card statement arrives.
analogy.breaks: Carts have fixed prices; cloud costs depend on usage too.

example.title: The missed change

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: ~$21,000/month increase hidden in a one-line diff.

example.outcome: why cost must be visible in review.

check.q: Why is the cloud bill a poor feedback mechanism for engineers?
check.a: It arrives weeks later, aggregated, after the change's author has moved on, so it rarely changes behaviour.

cloud-pricing-fundamentals-why-estimatio.core: Cloud prices depend on many dimensions: resource type and size, region, OS and licence, purchase model (on-demand, reserved, savings plans, spot), and usage-based components (GB transferred, requests, storage-hours, IOPS). IaC describes the resources but not their usage, so estimates are exact for fixed costs and approximate for usage-based ones unless you supply usage assumptions.

first_principles.problem: An estimate shows $0 for an S3 bucket and a NAT gateway's data processing, which later cost $4,000/month.
truths: Discounts happen at the billing layer.

analogy.title: Estimating a phone bill
analogy.story: The plan fee is known; calls and roaming depend on how you use it.
analogy.breaks: Phone plans are simple; clouds have millions of SKUs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Without usage data, half the bill is invisible.

check.q: Why can't IaC alone give an exact monthly cost?
check.a: It defines resources but not their usage (traffic, requests, storage growth), and discounts apply at billing.

the-tool-infracost.core: Infracost parses Terraform (HCL directly or plan JSON), maps each resource to price SKUs via its cloud pricing API, and outputs a monthly cost breakdown. `infracost diff` compares against a baseline to show the cost delta of a change. A usage file (infracost-usage.yml) supplies estimates for usage-based items such as Lambda requests or S3 GB, and it supports AWS, Azure and GCP.

first_principles.problem: Engineers have no quick way to see the cost of a Terraform change locally.

analogy.title: A quantity surveyor
analogy.story: They read architectural plans and price every material line by line, flagging items priced by usage.
analogy.breaks: Surveyors adjust for negotiated discounts; Infracost uses list prices by default.

example.title: Local diff

code.text:
infracost breakdown --path . --format json --out-file base.json   # on main
git checkout feature/bigger-nodes
infracost diff --path . --compare-to base.json
# ~ aws_eks_node_group.main
#   +$21,000 ($1,400 → $22,400)
# Monthly cost change: +$21,000 (+1500%)

example.outcome: cost as a local feedback loop.

check.a: The cost of the current code against a baseline (usually main), showing the monthly cost change per resource.

workflow-the-pull-request-comment.core: The biggest impact comes from CI: on every PR that touches IaC, Infracost computes the diff against main and posts or updates one comment showing the monthly cost change per project and resource. Reviewers see cost next to the code diff, making it part of the conversation ('do we need 8xlarge?') at the moment the change is cheapest to alter.

first_principles.problem: Engineers forget to run cost tools locally, so expensive changes still slip through.

analogy.title: A price tag on every item in the cart
analogy.story: You see the cost as you add things, not later.
analogy.breaks: Price tags are exact; usage costs are estimates.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every IaC PR shows its monthly cost delta.

check.q: Why use --behavior=update for the PR comment?
check.a: It edits one comment per PR instead of adding a new one on every push, keeping the thread readable.

cost-policies-automating-cost-governance.core: Visibility can be followed by enforcement. Cost policies evaluate Infracost JSON with OPA, Sentinel or Infracost guardrails, for example: block if the monthly increase exceeds $1,000 without FinOps approval, require Graviton instance families, forbid gp2 volumes, or require cost-center tags. Use tiers (warn, require approval, block) so policies guide rather than obstruct.

first_principles.problem: Visibility alone doesn't stop a team from repeatedly merging large cost increases without approval.
truths: Hard blocks frustrate if too strict.

analogy.title: A company expense policy
analogy.story: Small expenses auto-approve, larger ones need a manager, and some items are never allowed.
analogy.breaks: Expense policies are reviewed after spend; cost policies act before.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Big increases need approval; inefficient choices flagged.

code.text:
package infracost
import rego.v1

deny contains msg if {
  delta := to_number(input.diffTotalMonthlyCost)
  delta > 1000
  msg := sprintf("Monthly cost increase $%.0f exceeds $1000; needs FinOps approval", [delta])
}

warn contains msg if {
  some p in input.projects
  some r in p.breakdown.resources
  r.resourceType == "aws_ebs_volume"
  r.metadata.volumeType == "gp2"
  msg := sprintf("%s uses gp2; gp3 is ~20%% cheaper", [r.name])
}

check.q: Why tier cost policies instead of hard-blocking everything over a threshold?
check.a: Legitimate growth needs to proceed; tiers route big changes to approval while keeping teams unblocked.
